definitions.definition: The list of 108 Upaniṣads that Rāma teaches Hanumān in the Muktikā, one for each surviving Vedic branch, with their Vedas and peace-chants, taught as a graded curriculum for liberation (Māṇḍūkya → 10 → 32 → 108).

The editorial division of the non-principal Muktikā Upaniṣads into Sāmānya-Vedānta, Yoga, Sannyāsa, Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava groups, used by the Adyar Library series and later catalogues; it is not found in the Muktikā.

name: Four kinds of liberation (sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, sāyujya)

definitions.definition: Residence in the Lord's world, likeness of form, nearness and union — reached by devotion and meditation; the Muktikā counts them as lesser than kaivalya, which comes by knowledge alone; the Kalisantaraṇa promises all four to the reciter of the names.

In the minor Upaniṣads: the state of one who, knowing the Self, is freed while the body continues on the momentum of prārabdha; marked by freedom from 'I' and 'mine', from vāsanā and from the mind's properties (Muktikā 2; Varāha 4; Tejobindu 4); the dissolution of mind 'with form'.

Liberation at the fall of the body when prārabdha is exhausted — like pot-space merging with space or wind becoming still (Muktikā 1 prose, 2.76; Yogakuṇḍalī 3.34); the dissolution of mind 'without form'.

name: Destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth

definitions.definition: The Muktikā's triad (shared with the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka): the three must be practised together for liberation while living; the mind-tree has two seeds, prāṇa-vibration and vāsanā, and stopping one stops the other.

name: Mind as the cause of bondage and liberation

definitions.definition: Mind attached to objects binds, mind free of objects liberates (Amṛtabindu 2; Śāṭyāyanīya 1–3); mind alone is saṃsāra (Maitreya 1.5).

The unstruck sound heard within when breath and mind are stilled; listened to in stages from loud to subtle it absorbs the mind 'like milk in water'; its end is the soundless Brahman and the state beyond mind; in the Yogaśikhā nāda is bindu and bindu is mind, and no mantra is higher than nāda.

relations.note: Listening to nāda dissolves mind into the state beyond mind.

definitions.definition: In the Yoga Upaniṣads: (1) the seed-essence of the body, white (Śiva) and red (Śakti), whose retention and union are sought (Dhyānabindu, Yogatattva, Yogaśikhā — summary-only); (2) the point of Oṃ; (3) identified with mind (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.5; Yogaśikhā 6.73).

The coiled power lying at the base of the suṣumnā, blocking the door to Brahman; awakened by fire, breath and mind she rises through the centres and knots to unite with Śiva in the crown; 'bondage for the ignorant, liberation for yogins'; in the Varāha the supreme power from which breath, fire, bindu, nāda and mind arise.

relations.note: Rising kuṇḍalinī pierces the three knots (the knots obstruct her path).

definitions.definition: Six centres (mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddhi, ājñā) in most Yoga Upaniṣads, with the thousand-petalled lotus above; the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa counts nine cakras, sixteen ādhāras; the Yogaśikhā adds four pīṭhas (Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna); counts and attributes differ between texts.

72,000 channels spread from the kanda near the navel; ten or fourteen are principal (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, sarasvatī, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, alambusā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī, vāruṇī, viśvodarī, payasvinī); the suṣumnā is the path of liberation; iḍā carries the moon, piṅgalā the sun.

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna and the five minor — nāga (belching), kūrma (blinking), kṛkara (sneezing, hunger), devadatta (yawning, sleep), dhanañjaya (remains after death); each has a seat and function.
Knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra on the path of the suṣumnā, pierced by kuṇḍalinī through yoga and the grace of guru and god (Yogakuṇḍalī 1; Varāha 5; Brahmavidyā).

Inner (kuṇḍalinī, inner sound, blue light between the eyes), outer (colours and lights in space before the nose and above the head) and intermediate (the sequence of voids) — the objects of tāraka-yoga in the Advayatāraka and Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa.

Spaces seen in the intermediate target: ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa and paramākāśa (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 4.1), or the guṇa-less space, supreme space, great space, space of principles and space of the sun (Advayatāraka) — order and names differ.

Tāraka ('what makes one cross') is the yoga of lights and targets, with and without form; its later part is amanaska, the mind-less state in which the mind becomes 'like an udder after milking' (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 1.3, 3.1–2).

relations.note: Tāraka culminates in the mind-less (amanaska/unmanī) state.

name: Unmanī / manonmanī — the state beyond mind

definitions.definition: The state in which mind has dissolved (unmanībhāva); reached by nāda and tāraka; beyond merit and sin; the supreme state of Viṣṇu (Amṛtabindu 4; Nādabindu 48; Yogaśikhā 6.61; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa).

name: The fourth and beyond the fourth (turīya, turīyātīta)

definitions.definition: The minor Upaniṣads extend the Māṇḍūkya's four states to five (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth, beyond the fourth), place them in the body (navel/heart, throat, palate, brows, crown) and in the heart lotus, and in the sixteen-measured praṇava map sixteen states; the turīyātīta is also the name of the highest renouncer.
Both dissolve the mind, but in sleep it dissolves into tamas and does not liberate; in samādhi the world dissolves into the witness-consciousness (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 2.3).

Śubhecchā, vicāraṇā, tanumānasī, sattvāpatti, asaṃsakti, padārthabhāvanā, turyagā (Varāha 4; Akṣi 2; Mahā 5; cf. Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); mapped in the Varāha onto the measures of Oṃ and onto degrees of knowers of Brahman.
Seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep (Mahā 5, following the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha).

name: The four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja)

definitions.definition: One yoga divided in practice into four (Yogatattva 19); for practitioners of dull, middling and superior capacity (Varāha 5.10); in the Yogaśikhā four inner stages of one great yoga, each reinterpreted (mantra as reversed haṃsa, haṭha as union of sun and moon, laya as union of knower and supreme, rāja as union of rajas and retas).

name: The four stages of yoga (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti)

definitions.definition: Beginning, the 'pot' stage in which breaths, mind and selves unite, familiarity (kuṇḍalinī in the suṣumnā), and completion (natural yoga, liberation while living) — Yogatattva 20ff.; Varāha 5.71–75.

name: The limbs of yoga in the Yoga Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The Yoga Upaniṣads give six-limbed (Amṛtanāda — with tarka; Dhyānabindu; Yogacūḍāmaṇi), eight-limbed (Darśana, Śāṇḍilya, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa, Varāha, Yogatattva) and fifteen-limbed (Tejobindu) schemes, often with a second, knowledge-based definition of each limb.

name: Limbs of yoga redefined as knowledge

definitions.definition: In the Tejobindu, Triśikhi, Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and Darśana each limb is given an inner Vedāntic meaning — e.g. prāṇāyāma as seeing all as Brahman, āsana as indifference, dhyāna as 'so'ham' — alongside or instead of the bodily practice.

The claim of the Yogatattva and Yogaśikhā that knowledge without yoga and yoga without knowledge cannot liberate, and that both must be practised; contrasted with the Muktikā and Mahāvākya, where knowledge alone liberates.

Yamas: non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, rectitude, forbearance, fortitude, moderate diet, purity; niyamas: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, hearing doctrine, modesty, discernment, japa, vows (Śāṇḍilya, Darśana, Triśikhi, Varāha).

Varāha 1's enumeration of 96 tattvas: the 24 Sāṃkhya principles plus elements, bodies, states, six modifications, six waves, six sheaths, six enemies, three jīvas, guṇas, karmas, actions, inner functions, four sublime attitudes and fourteen deities; the Pāśupatabrahma makes the 96 the haṃsa's sacred thread.
The breath's natural sound — ha going out, sa coming in — repeated 21,600 times a day without effort; knowing it gives liberation (Dhyānabindu 61–65; Yogacūḍāmaṇi 31–35; Haṃsa).

name: Haṃsa — the swan / the self as breath-mantra

definitions.definition: The inner self as the 'swan' that moves with the breath (haṃ-sa), reversed as so'ham 'I am He'; meditated as a bird with fire and moon as wings; its knowledge (haṃsa-vidyā) is called the only means to liberation (Brahmavidyā) and the inner sacrifice (Pāśupatabrahma); also the name of the third kind of renouncer.

relations.note: Viewed as a mantra the haṃsa is the ajapā-gāyatrī.

definitions.definition: Oṃ analysed into three measures plus the half-measure (with Vedas, fires, worlds, deities, guṇas and colours), into twelve measures with destinies at death (Nādabindu), and sixteen measures ending in parā (Nāradaparivrājaka 8; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

name: Destiny according to the measure of Oṃ at death

definitions.definition: Nādabindu 12–16: one who dies while dwelling on each of the twelve measures attains a corresponding birth or world, the last giving the eternal Brahman.

name: The levels of speech (parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī)

definitions.definition: Speech sprouts in parā, leafs in paśyantī, buds in madhyamā and blossoms in vaikharī; reversed, sound dissolves (Yogakuṇḍalī 3.18–19); from the power at the base arise all letters, mantras, scriptures and the seven notes (Yogaśikhā 3).
Ciṇī, ciñciṇī, bell, conch, lute, cymbal, flute, mṛdaṅga, bherī, thunder — heard in order, each with its effect; the tenth is practised (Haṃsa 4).

name: The petals of the heart lotus and the moods

definitions.definition: The mind's dispositions follow the petal of the eight-petalled heart lotus on which the jīva rests — virtue, sleep, cruelty, sin, play, movement, love, charity — with the centre as dispassion or all-knowing (Haṃsa; Dhyānabindu).

name: Three kinds of teacher (codaka, bodhaka, mokṣada)

definitions.definition: The one who points out the path, the one who shows the place, the one who grants the supreme (Brahmavidyā 51–53).

name: The guru in the minor Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The guru removes darkness ('gu' darkness, 'ru' its remover) and is the supreme Brahman (Advayatāraka); he is Hari (Brahmavidyā), Brahmā-Viṣṇu-Sadāśiva (Yogaśikhā 5); his word breaks the pot that hides the lamp; without his grace the natural state is hard to reach (Varāha 2.76).

The teachings are to be given only to a calm, devoted, well-tested disciple or son — never to the unbeliever, ungrateful or unqualified (Muktikā 1.40–49; Subāla 16; Nirvāṇa; Mahāvākya; Yogaśikhā 2.2–3, 'after twelve years of service').

Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues (calm, restraint, withdrawal, forbearance, faith, concentration) and longing for liberation — prerequisites for study of the Upaniṣads (Muktikā prose; Varāha 2).

name: The bird's path and the ant's path

definitions.definition: Śuka's path (vihaṅgama): immediate liberation through inquiry; Vāmadeva's path (pipīlikā): gradual liberation through yoga over births (Varāha 4.34–42).

name: The monkey's way and the crow's way

definitions.definition: Yogaśikhā 1.140–144: gradual completion within one body (monkey), or rebirth and swift fruition through a siddha guru (crow).
The Yogaśikhā's claim that the body must be 'cooked' by the fire of yoga; the unripe body of the mere knower is subject to rebirth.

Powers arise from practice and concentration (far-hearing, far-seeing, invisibility, sky-travel, entering bodies); the Yogatattva calls them obstacles to be hidden; the Yogaśikhā distinguishes contrived from spontaneous powers and treats spontaneous powers as the test of a siddha.
Triśikhi 119–127: the cessation of throbbing at particular points of the limbs and failure to see the tip of one's tongue foretell the time of death.
Leaving the body with the breath through the crown so as not to return (Amṛtanāda 39; Kuṇḍikā); recorded summary-only.

name: The last thought decides the next state

definitions.definition: What one thinks at death determines what one becomes (Yogaśikhā 1.31; Nāradaparivrājaka 5).
For the knower, prārabdha karma continues to move the body but has no hold, like dream-objects after waking; knowledge destroys accumulated and future karma (Nādabindu 21–29).

name: The formation of the body in the womb

definitions.definition: The Garbha Upaniṣad's account of the body's elements and constituents, the embryo's monthly growth, and its memory and vow in the ninth month, forgotten at birth — the tradition's own account.

name: The after-death body built by the piṇḍas

definitions.definition: Piṇḍa Upaniṣad: the departed passes days in water, fire, space and wind, and the ten rice-balls successively build its new body.
'The body is a temple and the jīva in it is Śiva' (Maitreya 2.1; Skanda 10); the Yogaśikhā calls it Śiva's or Viṣṇu's temple; the Bhāvanā makes the body the Śrīcakra.

The sacred places are located within: Vārāṇasī between brows and nose, Prayāga in the heart, etc. (Darśana 4.48–59; Jābāla 2); the suṣumnā is the supreme tīrtha (Yogaśikhā 6); wandering to outer tīrthas is 'lowest of the low' (Maitreya 2.21).
Solstices, equinoxes, new moon and eclipses are the movements of breath between iḍā and piṅgalā and between the base and the head (Darśana 4.39–47; Śāṇḍilya 1.15).

Forms of the formless are imagined for the sake of worshippers (Rāmapūrvatāpanī 1.7); yogins see Śiva in the Self, images are for the ignorant (Darśana 4.59); for the renouncer image-worship leads to rebirth (Maitreya 2.26).

Rites internalized: the haṃsa as fire and praṇava as thread (Pāśupatabrahma), eating as oblation to the prāṇas (Prāṇāgnihotra), the world offered into the fire of knowledge (Sannyāsa 2.100), the renouncer's five inner sacrifices (Śāṭyāyanīya 12–17).
Outer, inner and supreme self (Ātma Upaniṣad); inner self Brahmā, supreme self Maheśvara, eternal self of all Viṣṇu (Rudrahṛdaya); the inner controller whose body is the elements (Subāla 7).

The jīva bound by ego is the paśu, the Lord is Paśupati; release from the bond (pāśa) through the pāśupata vow and ash (Atharvaśiras 5; Jābāli); 'bound by the husk it is paddy, without husk rice' (Skanda 6–7).
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva and Śiva of Viṣṇu (Skanda 8–9); whoever honours Govinda honours Śaṅkara (Rudrahṛdaya); the one Lord is Brahmā, Śiva, Indra and Viṣṇu (Kaivalya 8).
The Śākta Upaniṣads declare the Goddess — Devī, Tripurā, Sītā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī — to be Brahman, the primordial nature and the inner self; the great sayings are her (Bahvṛca).
The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā, as distinct from the one quarter that is the world (Tripādvibhūti-Mahānārāyaṇa, developing Ṛgveda 10.90.3).
Brahman has three forms: with parts (sakala), without parts (niṣkala) and both; its most manifest form is Dattātreya (Śāṇḍilya 3; Brahmavidyā 37–40).

U04 contribution: the minor Upaniṣads treat the four sayings as a secret initiatory teaching (Śukarahasya), assign one to each Veda and maṭha (Maṭhāmnāya), give them to the renouncer at initiation (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka) and read them as the Goddess (Bahvṛca).

Avimukta (Kāśī) is where Rudra gives the dying the tāraka — the mantra that carries across — so that they are freed; it is also located in the body between brows and nose (Jābāla 1–2; Muktikā 1.19–21; Rāmottaratāpanī; Tārasāra). The tāraka is identified variously as Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra.
The sixteen names 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare' taught by Brahmā to Nārada as the means of crossing Kali, bound by no rule (Kalisantaraṇa).

Leaving the ritual world and household to wander as a mendicant; in the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads true renunciation is the union of jīva and supreme Self (Maitreya 2.17), undertaken 'the very day one becomes dispassionate' (Jābāla 4); 'by renunciation alone some reached immortality' (Kaivalya 1.3).
Renunciation from dispassion, from knowledge, from knowledge-and-dispassion, and ritual renunciation (Nāradaparivrājaka 5); the Śāṭyāyanīya's four kinds of renouncer all keep Viṣṇu's marks.

name: Renunciation of the knower and of the seeker

definitions.definition: The knower (vidvat) renounces having realized; the seeker (vividiṣā) renounces in order to realize and keeps the insignia (Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; developed in Vidyāraṇya's Jīvanmuktiviveka).

Renunciation by one in mortal danger (ātura), by mind and speech alone, versus renunciation in due order (krama); ritual renunciation is 'occasioned' or 'unoccasioned' (Jābāla 5; Nāradaparivrājaka 3, 5).

Four (kuṭīcaka, bahūdaka, haṃsa, paramahaṃsa — Bhikṣuka, Āśrama, Śāṭyāyanīya) or six (adding turīyātīta and avadhūta — Nāradaparivrājaka 5; Sannyāsa 2), graded by freedom from marks and rules, food, bathing, worship and the world attained.

Staff (one or three), water-pot, sling, strainer, ochre or no cloth, shaven head, topknot and thread kept or abandoned; the texts differ on which marks are kept, and many say the true marks are inner (staff of knowledge, thread of the Self) and that marks do not liberate.

name: The inner topknot and sacred thread

definitions.definition: Knowledge is the topknot and the Self, Brahman or praṇava the sacred thread of the renouncer, replacing the outer ones (Jābāla 5; Brahma; Paramahaṃsa; Parabrahma; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.77–85).
Mādhūkara, prākpraṇīta, ayācita, tātkālika and upapanna (Sannyāsa 2.65–70).

Penances, śrāddhas including one's own, the virajā homa, placing the fires in oneself, the declaration renouncing the three desires, the gift of fearlessness, abandoning topknot and thread, and receiving praṇava and great saying from the guru — a ritual death to the world (Jābāla 4; Āruṇi 2–3; Nāradaparivrājaka 4.38; Kaṭharudra; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).

name: The renouncer's permitted modes of death

definitions.definition: The Jābāla and Kaṭharudra mention modes by which a renouncer may end life; recorded summary-only, with no guidance.

Eligibility rules: dispassion, the fourfold means, freedom from certain defects and statuses; the ineligible may renounce when at the point of death; texts differ on whether the unmarried may renounce and on consent of kin.
The knower who has transcended caste and stage and abides in the Self (Avadhūta 2; Kaivalya 2; Maitreya 1.13).

The highest renouncer, 'who has shaken off' saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, living without marks or rules, appearing child-like, mad or ghost-like (Avadhūta 1–2; Turīyātīta; Jābāla 6; Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 5).
The liberated renouncer's freedom from rule (Nirvāṇa; Avadhūta 33), qualified in the Avadhūta by the option of acting by scripture for the world's good.
Āśrama Upaniṣad: four kinds each of student, householder, forest-dweller and wanderer.
Not the jīva, body, birth, learning, action or dharmic deeds, but one who has realized the non-dual Self and is free of faults (Vajrasūci); caste is imagined for convention (Nirālamba).
